questions.q: You earn {s} a year. Your employer pays the minimum 3% of qualifying earnings (pay between £6,240 and £50,270). How much does your employer pay in a year?
questions.why: Qualifying earnings are {s} − £6,240. 3% of that is {answer}.

questions.q: Your pension uses relief at source. You pay in {p}. How much lands in your pot once 20% basic-rate relief is added?
questions.why: What you pay is 80% of the gross amount: {p} ÷ 0.8 = {answer}.

questions.q: Who must be automatically enrolled into a workplace pension?
options: Workers aged 22 to State Pension age earning over £10,000 a year
Everyone with a job, from age 16
questions.why: The trigger is age 22 to State Pension age and earnings over £10,000. Younger or lower-paid workers can usually ask to join.

questions.q: If you opt out of your workplace pension, your employer pays you their contribution as extra wages instead.
questions.why: The employer contribution only exists if you're in the scheme. Opt out and it's simply lost.

questions.q: From 6 April 2028, what's the earliest age most people can take money from a workplace pension?
questions.why: The normal minimum pension age rises from 55 to 57 on 6 April 2028. The State Pension age is separate (66, rising to 67).

questions.q: How many qualifying years of National Insurance do you normally need for the full new State Pension?
questions.why: 35 qualifying years for the full amount, and at least 10 to get any.

questions.q: Match each pension to how it works.
pairs: Paid by the government, based on your NI record
You and your employer pay in while you work
A personal pension you open and run yourself
A guaranteed income bought with your pension pot
questions.why: Most people's retirement income combines the State Pension with workplace and personal savings.

questions.q: Same contributions and growth, all stopping at 67. Put these starting ages in order of final pot, biggest first.
questions.why: Earlier contributions get more years to compound, and the last years grow the most.

questions.q: When you start taking a workplace pension, how much can usually be taken tax-free?
questions.why: Usually 25% tax-free (within an overall limit); the rest is taxed as income when you take it.

questions.q: A friend wants to opt out of their workplace pension to have more money now. Explain what they'd give up.
questions.model: They'd give up the employer's contribution, which they only get by staying in, and the tax relief, which together roughly double what they pay. They'd also lose decades of compound growth on that money, which is worth most when started young.
questions.why: Opting out loses the employer money and tax relief today, plus growth later.

tests.answer: They lose the employer contribution and the tax relief, and all the compound growth over the years.
They lose the free money their employer pays in.

questions.q: Explain why starting a pension at 22 rather than 32 can make a difference of tens of thousands of pounds.

ideas.label: The money gets 10 more years to compound
The final years add the most growth, so missing years costs a lot

questions.model: Money paid in at 22 gets 10 more years to compound, and the growth is biggest in the final years when the pot is largest, so a later start loses the most valuable growth.
questions.why: Time in the pot matters more than the amount.

tests.answer: It has ten more years to compound and the growth is biggest at the end.
Pensions pay more to young people.
